docs.title: Terminate Optimizer Worker Processes
docs.text: This document describes a targeted script for terminating optimizer worker processes. It avoids killing unrelated processes that merely contain the word hyper in their command line.

docs.title: Important safety note
docs.text:
Stop the active optimizer sweep in the dashboard before running the script. Otherwise, the sweep manager may immediately create replacement workers.

The script sends SIGTERM first, waits briefly, and then sends SIGKILL to remaining matching processes. The second signal also removes workers that are stuck in the stopped (T) process state.

Completed optimizer results remain persisted on disk and can be resumed after the dashboard is restarted.

docs.title: Script
docs.text:
Save the following as kill_optimizer_workers.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Terminate Python module processes matching PROCESS_SUBJECT.
# The first positional argument takes precedence over the environment variable.
# Example:
#   ./kill_optimizer_workers.sh 'optimizer\.hyperopt_runner'
#   PROCESS_SUBJECT='optimizer\.hyperopt_runner' ./kill_optimizer_workers.sh

set -u

PROCESS_SUBJECT="${1:-${PROCESS_SUBJECT:-optimizer\.hyperopt_runner}}"
PYTHON_EXEC_RE='(^|/)python(3)?$'

optimizer_pids() {
  ps -eo pid=,args= |
    awk -v subject="$PROCESS_SUBJECT" -v python_exec="$PYTHON_EXEC_RE" '
      $2 ~ python_exec &&
      $0 ~ ("(^|[[:space:]])-m[[:space:]]+" subject "([[:space:]]|$)") {
        print $1
      }
    '
}

terminate_processes() {
  local signal="$1"
  local pids

  pids="$(optimizer_pids)"

  if [[ -z "$pids" ]]; then
    echo "No matching optimizer processes found."
    return
  fi

  echo "Sending SIG${signal} to:"
  echo "$pids"

  # PIDs come directly from ps and are numeric.
  kill "-${signal}" $pids 2>/dev/null || true
}

echo "Matching processes before termination:"
optimizer_pids

terminate_processes TERM

# Give normal shutdown a moment to complete.
sleep 2

# Remove workers that did not respond, including stopped (T-state) workers.
terminate_processes KILL

echo
if [[ -z "$(optimizer_pids)" ]]; then
  echo "All matching processes have been removed."
else
  echo "Some matching processes remain:"
  optimizer_pids
fi

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Make the script executable:

chmod +x kill_optimizer_workers.sh

Terminate the optimizer workers:

./kill_optimizer_workers.sh

The default target is:

optimizer.hyperopt_runner

To pass a different module without editing the script:

./kill_optimizer_workers.sh 'another\.module_name'

The same value can be supplied through the environment:

PROCESS_SUBJECT='another\.module_name' ./kill_optimizer_workers.sh

The positional argument takes precedence over the environment variable.

docs.title: Why ps -aux | grep hyper | wc -l is unreliable
docs.text:
That command also counts the grep process itself and any unrelated command containing hyper. The script matches the exact Python module invocation:

python -m optimizer.hyperopt_runner

It therefore does not terminate unrelated dashboard, exchange, or test processes.

docs.title: After termination
docs.text: Restart the dashboard so the current optimizer concurrency settings are loaded. Then resume the persisted sweep through the dashboard or the supported /api/optimizer/sweep/resume endpoint.

docs.title: Graphene Supercapacitors
docs.text: Graphene supercapacitors are advanced energy‑storage devices that use graphene as the electrode material to dramatically improve the performance of traditional supercapacitors. The core idea: supercapacitors store energy electrostatically, not chemically like batteries — and graphene maximizes the speed, power, and lifetime of this process.

docs.title: ⚡ Short answer
docs.text: A graphene supercapacitor is a high‑power energy storage device that uses graphene’s enormous surface area and conductivity to store electric charge extremely fast, deliver huge bursts of power, and survive millions of cycles — but with lower energy density than batteries. Graphene improves supercapacitors by increasing surface area, ion accessibility, conductivity, and mechanical stability, enabling next‑generation high‑power applications. RSC Publishing eureka.patsnap.com

docs.title: 🧩 How a supercapacitor works (in simple terms)
docs.text:
Supercapacitors store energy in an electric double layer (EDL): - Two electrodes (usually carbon‑based) - An electrolyte with ions - A separator

When voltage is applied, ions accumulate on the electrode surfaces → forming a double layer → storing charge physically, not chemically.

This is why supercapacitors: - Charge in seconds - Deliver very high power - Last millions of cycles - But store less total energy than batteries

docs.title: 🧪 Why graphene makes supercapacitors far better
docs.text: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms with extreme properties:

docs.title: 1. Huge surface area → more charge storage
docs.text: Graphene’s theoretical surface area is 2,630 m²/g, far higher than activated carbon (100–200 m²/g). This allows theoretical capacitance up to ~550 F/g, far above conventional materials. eureka.patsnap.com

docs.title: 2. Very high electrical conductivity → fast charging/discharging
docs.text: Pristine graphene conductivity exceeds 1,700 S/m, compared to <10 S/m for activated carbon. This reduces internal resistance (ESR) and boosts power density. eureka.patsnap.com

docs.title: 3. Mechanical strength → long lifetime
docs.text: Graphene’s tensile strength (~130 GPa) and stiffness (Young’s modulus ~1 TPa) prevent structural degradation over millions of cycles. eureka.patsnap.com

docs.title: 4. Tunability through doping and composites
docs.text:
Graphene can be combined with: - Metal oxides (MOs) - Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) - Heteroatom doping (N, B, S)

These improve ion diffusion, charge transport, and energy density. RSC Publishing

docs.title: 🔋 Types of graphene supercapacitors
docs.text: Graphene can be used in several architectures:

docs.title: 1. Electric Double‑Layer Capacitors (EDLCs)
docs.text: Pure graphene or graphene‑derived carbon. - Highest power - Fastest charge - Longest cycle life RSC Publishing

docs.title: 2. Pseudocapacitors
docs.text: Graphene + metal oxides (MnO₂, RuO₂) or conductive polymers. - Higher energy density - Slightly lower cycle life RSC Publishing

docs.title: 3. Asymmetric supercapacitors (ASC)
docs.text: Graphene negative electrode + pseudocapacitive positive electrode. - Balanced energy + power RSC Publishing

docs.title: 🚀 Performance advantages
docs.text: Feature Graphene Supercapacitor Conventional Supercapacitor Energy density Higher (due to SSA & composites) Lower Power density Extremely high High Charge time Seconds Seconds Cycle life Millions Millions Conductivity Very high Moderate Heat generation Very low Low

docs.title: 🔧 Where graphene supercapacitors are used
docs.text:
Graphene supercapacitors are ideal for high‑power, fast‑charge applications:

  • Regenerative braking in EVs
  • Bus/tram acceleration systems
  • Grid buffering for renewables
  • Industrial cranes/elevators
  • UPS systems
  • High‑power electronics
  • Wearable/flexible electronics (future)

Skeleton Technologies (Estonia) is a leading commercial developer using curved graphene to boost performance. youtube.com youtube.com

docs.title: 🧱 Limitations
docs.text: Even with graphene, supercapacitors still have lower energy density than lithium batteries. Research focuses on: - Doping - Composite formation - 3D graphene aerogels - Hybrid battery‑capacitor systems RSC Publishing

docs.title: 🧭 Bottom line
docs.text:
Graphene supercapacitors are not a battery replacement yet, but they are a revolution in high‑power energy storage. They excel at: - Fast charging - High power bursts - Long lifetime - High efficiency

And graphene is the key material enabling the next leap in performance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A phase-change battery (PCM thermal battery) stores heat by melting and solidifying a special material. During this phase transition, the material absorbs or releases large amounts of energy at a constant temperature, enabling compact and stable thermal storage.

docs.title: Charging (Heat Absorption)
docs.text: A heat source—typically a heat pump or PV-powered electric element—heats the phase-change material (PCM) to its melting point. As the PCM melts, it absorbs a large amount of latent heat without increasing in temperature.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Once melted, the PCM remains in a liquid state as long as its temperature stays above the melting point. Because latent heat storage is highly efficient, PCM modules can store much more energy per liter than water.

docs.title: Discharging (Heat Release)
docs.text: When heat is needed, the PCM cools and solidifies. During solidification, it releases the stored latent heat at a constant temperature, making it ideal for domestic hot water and low-temperature heating systems.

docs.title: Why PCM Is Better Than a Traditional Water Buffer
docs.text:
• High energy density: PCM stores 3–5× more energy per liter than water.
  • Constant output temperature: PCM maintains a fixed temperature (e.g., 55°C) during discharge.
  • Compact design: A 50-liter PCM module can replace a 200-liter water tank.
  • Perfect for PV integration: Excess solar power can be converted into stored heat efficiently.
  • Reduced peak electrical load: Heat pumps can operate when COP is highest, lowering grid demand.

docs.title: Typical Home Integration
docs.text: A PCM battery is usually a compact module (30–80 liters) connected to a heat pump or electric heater. It provides thermal storage for domestic hot water or heating and can be controlled by smart home systems.

docs.title: Example: PCM at 55°C
docs.text:
• Melting point: 55°C
  • Storage capacity: 3–6 kWh per 50 liters
  • Applications: Domestic hot water, low-temperature heating

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A phase-change battery stores heat by melting and solidifying a special material, enabling compact, efficient, and stable thermal energy storage—ideal for modern heat pumps and solar-powered homes.
